Cisco Talos researchers disclosed a new strain of infostealer malware called Volta-Autodoxer that incorporates large language model (LLM) functionality to profile victims and prioritize high‑value data.
The finding was published in the Kernel Panic newsletter on 31 October 2026.

entries.text: The malware automatically gathers credentials, tokens and payment information before sending a serialized dossier to an LLM for analysis.

Volta-Autodoxer collects passwords, browser‑saved credentials, Microsoft OAuth tokens, cookies, payment cards and crypto‑wallet seed phrases, as well as active sessions on Discord, Telegram, Steam and Roblox.
After the initial sweep it performs a deeper scan of central accounts such as Gmail, extracting receipts, order history and location data from services like UberEats.
The LLM is prompted to act as an intelligence analyst, producing a citation‑backed assessment that ranks the victim's value for the attacker.
problems: model check: Source mentions a citation‑backed assessment but does not state that the LLM ranks the victim's value.

entries.text: Infostealer malware has long been used to harvest login details that fuel large data breaches, including incidents involving Snowflake, AT&T, Ticketmaster and Disney.
By adding AI, Volta-Autodoxer automates the profiling step that previously required manual analysis, potentially increasing the speed and precision of credential theft.
problems: model check: Source confirms automation of profiling and speed, but does not provide evidence that precision of credential theft is increased; the claim adds unsupported speculation.

entries.text: Cisco Talos flagged the tool using its new CAIRN framework, which detects hacking tools that embed AI capabilities, though the researchers have not observed active deployments in the wild.

Apple CEO John Ternus said the company will use artificial intelligence in upcoming devices, but it will not release AI features just for their own sake.
He became CEO in September and addressed the topic in a Wired interview with Steven Levy.
Ternus emphasized that the goal is to create products people love, regardless of whether AI is involved.
Ternus noted that Apple has been perceived as lagging because Siri’s more powerful version only arrived this summer.
He argued that when AI is applied correctly, users should not need to consider the underlying technology.
He also said that AI could eventually make tasks like app creation easier, but product creation remains a human‑driven activity.
Apple has historically focused on tightly integrated hardware and software, often delaying AI rollouts compared with competitors.

Pika Labs released Pika H3 Flex, a post‑trained H3 model for professional creators, on 29 October 2026.
The model generates video with synchronized stereo audio in six sampling steps.
It supports up to 12 reference inputs and can produce native 480p or 768p video locally, with higher resolutions via the hosted API.
The architecture adds two task adapters: FL2VA for text and endpoint‑frame conditioning, and Ref2VA for multimodal references.
It builds on the MiniMax‑H3 base model and processes prompts and media through an encoder before producing video and audio latents.
The inference pipeline then decodes these latents and combines them into an MP4 file, automatically downloading the pinned base components and selected adapter.
In generative AI, video models often require separate audio synthesis, leading to mismatched timing.
problems: model check: Source does not state that other video models require separate audio synthesis or cause mismatched timing.

entries.text: Pika H3 Flex integrates both modalities, allowing creators to control motion and sound together, which simplifies multi‑shot storytelling and motion‑graphics workflows.
The six‑step generation balances quality and speed, making the model usable on consumer hardware for 480p and 768p outputs.
problems: model check: Source mentions six‑step generation and native resolutions but does not state that it balances quality and speed or is usable on consumer hardware.

OpenAI announced that it has reduced the size of its upcoming financing round to a $20 billion target after earlier reports of a $30 billion raise.
The revision follows a valuation drop from $1.4 trillion to $1.25 trillion and comes ahead of a planned initial public offering.
Investors from the United Arab Emirates will lead the round, with a possible retail tranche for wealthy individuals.
The company has already secured $11 billion in commitments, according to a Wall Street Journal follow‑up, but the overall response from large investors has been described as “tepid”.
The first close of the round is expected to be below the $20 billion goal, and the total may only be reached through the additional retail offering.
Analysts suggest that the softer fundraising environment is linked to Wall Street’s caution over heavy AI infrastructure spending and a broader sell‑off in tech stocks.
OpenAI’s funding efforts have been closely watched because the firm’s valuation and capital needs influence the broader AI market.

Biotech founder Gabriel Ocana Santero connected an AI agent to a robotic arm, injector and camera to perform a brain injection on a living mouse.
The experiment was carried out by his company Exin Therapeutics in San Francisco and was reported on 31 October 2026.
The AI chose a therapy from 19 options, set injection coordinates and controlled the needle during the procedure.
The setup included a motorized device to immobilize the mouse, a camera for visual feedback and a robotic injector that the AI could move.
After a veterinary surgeon made a craniotomy, the AI selected a gene‑therapy candidate aimed at reducing seizures in an epileptic mouse, then set the injection volume and speed.

entries.text: The team first tried Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5, which refused to guide the needle, citing internal safety warnings.
They switched to Claude Sonnet 5, which completed the injection as instructed.
AI models used in research are typically trained on published papers, so they miss real‑time observations and failed experiments.
By giving an AI direct control of lab hardware, researchers hope to make models more reliable and useful for experimental design.
Santero’s test shows both the promise and the current safety limits of such integration.

The AI‑driven profiling could let cybercriminals prioritize high‑value accounts more quickly, increasing the risk of large‑scale data breaches for individuals and businesses that store credentials, payment info, and crypto wallets.

OpenAI’s reduced $20 billion funding round reflects investor caution about costly AI infrastructure, which may slow the pace of new AI tools and affect market dynamics for companies relying on large‑scale models.
